cards.text: Ezekiel, a priest living among the exiles by the Kebar River, gets another word from the LORD (Ezekiel 1:1-3). Last time, God had him shave his head and beard with a sword and divide the hair into thirds, a picture of judgment on Jerusalem for her detestable idols (Ezekiel 5:1-12). Now God, who calls him son of man, tells him to turn his face toward something and prophesy against it.

cards.question: God tells Ezekiel to set his face against something and prophesy against it. What is it?

cards.text: So Ezekiel has to preach to the mountains and hills, the ravines and valleys. And I thought the expired coupon in my old junk drawer was a TOUGH crowd.
God's message for them: 'I am about to bring a sword against you.' And then He says there's something on those mountains He will destroy.

cards.question: God is bringing a sword against the mountains of Israel. What does He say He will destroy there?

cards.text: Then the list keeps going: altars demolished, incense altars SMASHED. And I thought it was loud the day I dropped a whole stack of cookie trays.

cards.question: On the mountains of Israel, God says He will cast down their slain right in front of their ___.
God says He will scatter the Israelites' bones around their altars.

cards.text: And it's not just the mountains, friend. Wherever they live, the cities will be laid waste, the idols smashed and obliterated, and their works blotted out.

cards.question: When the slain fall among the people of Israel, what does God say they will come to know?

cards.text: After all that sword and smashing, the message turns on one little word: 'Yet.' Friend, after years in the back of a junk drawer, I will take a 'yet' ANY day of the week.

cards.question: After that word 'Yet,' God says every last person in Israel will fall by the sword.

cards.text: A remnant escapes the sword, but they end up scattered among the nations, carried off as captives. I bet they feel like I did in that drawer: far from home, wondering who still remembers who.

cards.question: Far away in the nations where they've been carried captive, who will the survivors of Israel remember?

cards.text: They'll remember how He was grieved by their adulterous hearts that turned away from Him, and by their eyes that lusted after idols.

cards.question: Remembering how they grieved the LORD, the survivors will ___ themselves for the evil they have done.
God says His warning that He would bring this calamity on Israel was an empty threat.

cards.text: Next, God gives Ezekiel stage directions. Remember the haircut? This prophet is no stranger to acting it out.

cards.question: Because of all the wicked abominations of the house of Israel, what does God tell Ezekiel to do?

answers.text: Clap his hands and stomp his feet
Tear his robe and sit in ashes
Lie on his side for many days

cards.text: He's also to cry out 'Alas!' for the house of Israel, who will fall by sword and famine and plague. Me, I clap and stomp when a batch comes out golden, so this is a WHOLE different kind of clapping.

cards.question: In God's picture of sword, famine and plague, the one who is far off gets away safe.

cards.text: That line comes back: 'Then you will know that I am the LORD.' Their slain will lie among their idols around their altars, on every high hill and under every green tree and leafy oak.

cards.question: The high hills and leafy oaks where the slain will lie were the very places where the people had done what?

answers.text: Offered fragrant incense to their idols

cards.text: Last, God says He will stretch out His hand against them and make the land a desolate waste.

cards.question: How much of the land does God say He will make a desolate waste?

cards.text: From the wilderness all the way to Diblah. And the message ends on that line one last time: 'Then they will know that I am the LORD.'

findings.problem: The joke doesn't land. The core action is speaking to mountains and valleys, an audience that can't answer back. The expired coupon is a talking drawer-mate described in the backstory as one that 'still believed in itself,' an optimist rather than a tough crowd. A stranger would ask why a coupon is a tough crowd.

rule.text: 2. The everyday comparison must have the same action. ... 4. It clicks instantly for any adult, with no explaining. 5. If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: The card says Ezekiel has to 'preach' to the mountains. The text calls it prophesying ('prophesy against them,' 6:2) and saying ('You are to say,' 6:3), not preaching.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The comparison doesn't share the core action. God deliberately demolishes the idolatrous altars, but dropping cookie trays is an accident and is only about noise, which the text never mentions. The joke also reuses the 'And I thought...' setup from card 3, so it reads as a formula. It sits next to a verse about the slain being cast down before idols, and the light noise gag doesn't fit that moment.

rule.text: 1. Find the core action in the fact: running away, waiting, being outnumbered, preparing, being surprised. 2. The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The question says the slain fall 'among the people of Israel.' The text says 'The slain will fall among you,' inside a message addressed to the mountains, hills, ravines and valleys (6:3). The card picks one meaning of 'you' that the text leaves open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'praise' makes the line 'praise themselves for the evil they have done' right after remembering how they grieved the LORD. That isn't believable, and it reads as a throwaway option next to 'loathe' and 'forgive.'

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The card says Ezekiel is to cry out 'Alas!' 'for the house of Israel.' The text gives the reason: 'because of all the wicked abominations of the house of Israel' (6:11). The card changes the stated reason into crying out on Israel's behalf.

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.
